clinicalPearls: Rare autosomal recessive form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia caused by variants in CYP17A1, the single enzyme performing both 17-alpha-hydroxylase and 17,20-lyase reactions.
The enzyme block impairs cortisol and all sex-steroid synthesis while leaving the mineralocorticoid pathway intact and overactive.
Classic triad is hypertension, hypokalaemia and hypogonadism, typically recognised around the expected time of puberty.
46,XY individuals usually present with a female or undervirilised external phenotype because androgen synthesis fails during fetal development.
46,XX individuals present with primary amenorrhoea, absent pubertal development and hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism.
Accumulated 11-deoxycorticosterone and corticosterone drive low-renin hypertension with potassium loss, mirroring the mineralocorticoid excess of 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency.
Cortisol deficiency is partially offset by corticosterone, which has weak glucocorticoid activity, so overt adrenal crisis is less typical than in other forms.
Isolated 17,20-lyase deficiency produces sex-steroid failure without the hypertension seen in the combined form.
reference.pathophysiology: 17-alpha-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase deficiency results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in CYP17A1, which encodes a single microsomal cytochrome P450 enzyme responsible for two sequential activities in both the adrenal cortex and the gonads. The 17-alpha-hydroxylase activity is required to convert pregnenolone and progesterone into their 17-hydroxylated forms en route to cortisol, while the 17,20-lyase activity is required to generate the C19 precursors of androgens and oestrogens. When the enzyme is deficient, cortisol and sex-steroid production are both impaired, but steroidogenesis is diverted into the mineralocorticoid pathway, which does not require 17-alpha-hydroxylation. The consequent overproduction of 11-deoxycorticosterone and corticosterone causes sodium retention, volume expansion, potassium wasting, metabolic alkalosis and suppression of renin and aldosterone, producing a low-renin hypertension. Loss of cortisol removes feedback inhibition and raises corticotrophin, which sustains the adrenal drive, while the failure of gonadal androgen and oestrogen synthesis causes hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism. Because corticosterone possesses modest glucocorticoid activity, symptomatic cortisol deficiency and salt-wasting crises are uncommon, and affected individuals frequently come to attention only when expected puberty fails to occur.
additionalDifferentials: Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (46,XY with female phenotype)
Gonadal dysgenesis and other causes of primary amenorrhoea
Primary hyperaldosteronism and other low-renin hypertensive syndromes

additionalInvestigations: Plasma renin activity and aldosterone (both suppressed)
Serum electrolytes for hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis
Karyotype with pelvic and gonadal imaging
redFlags: Adolescent with absent puberty and unexplained hypertension needing prompt endocrine evaluation
Severe hypokalaemia causing muscle weakness or cardiac arrhythmia
46,XY individual with intra-abdominal gonads carrying a risk of malignant transformation
Hypertensive end-organ damage in a young person
Diagnostic confusion delaying gender assignment and psychological support in a child with a disorder of sex development
reference.prognosis: With glucocorticoid replacement to suppress the overactive mineralocorticoid pathway, control of hypertension and hypokalaemia, and sex-steroid replacement to induce and maintain secondary sexual characteristics, long-term outlook is generally good. Fertility is severely limited, and prognosis depends on timely control of hypertension, appropriate management of dysgenetic or intra-abdominal gonads, and multidisciplinary care of the associated disorder of sex development.
pitfalls: Attributing primary amenorrhoea to a purely gynaecological cause and missing the associated hypertension and electrolyte disturbance.
Assuming a 46,XY infant is female and overlooking intra-abdominal testes that require monitoring or removal.
Expecting florid adrenal crisis; corticosterone provides partial glucocorticoid cover so crises are relatively uncommon.
Confusing the combined deficiency with isolated 17,20-lyase deficiency, which lacks hypertension.
Neglecting bone health and cardiovascular risk from long-standing hypogonadism and hypertension.
